column6: Those who lose property under pressure accept it joyfully because they know they have a better, abiding possession; this gives the commentary's better-and-more-lasting contrast a concrete setting of threatened choice.
Jesus contrasts food that perishes with food remaining into eternal life, directly framing worldly provision against what abides.
The world and its desire pass away, while the doer of God's will remains forever; it closely matches the rejected worldly preference and abiding good.
Paul distinguishes temporary visible things from eternal unseen things, supplying the same evaluative contrast that governs the two sides of the commentary's scale.
The maxim calls one hour of bliss in the world to come better than all life in this world, an explicit analogue to 87:17's comparison.
A tortured brother tells the king that the King of the universe will raise them to everlasting renewed life; it is a choice under a human tyrant for an enduring divine future.
Those awakening from the dust receive either everlasting life or everlasting abhorrence, furnishing both the enduring good and the enduring adverse fate developed in the commentary.
The final separation explicitly pairs eternal punishment with eternal life, the same warning that permanence can belong to punishment as well as blessedness.
The youngest brother contrasts his brothers' short suffering and God's everlasting-life covenant with the king's coming punishment, sharpening the commentary's temporal-versus-lasting judgment.
Tortured faithful people refuse release in order to obtain a better resurrection, a direct instance of choosing costly fidelity for a superior future.

column5: life in this world / eternal life
column6: Loving one's life in this world loses it, while relinquishing it keeps it for eternal life; the verse makes the commentary's preference an existential choice.
The question about gaining the whole world while forfeiting one's life concentrates worldly acquisition and ultimate loss into the commentary's two-sided valuation.
Believers have no abiding city here but seek the coming one, an especially close counterpart to the claim that the other life is what remains.
This world is a vestibule before the world to come, where one must prepare to enter the banquet hall; it turns present life into a passage rather than the preferred destination.
The righteous may appear punished to observers, yet their hope is full of immortality, making present appearance a poor measure of lasting worth.

column5: rich man's good things / Lazarus's comfort
column6: Abraham recalls that the rich man received good things in life while Lazarus received bad, but their postmortem conditions are reversed; it tests what worldly “good” is worth.
Treasure on earth is subject to moth, corrosion, and theft, concretizing the commentary's claim that the worldly side is not what lasts.
Treasure in heaven escapes moth, corrosion, and theft, giving a durable alternative to the perishable possessions of the preceding verse.
The rich fool's life is demanded on the night he relies on accumulated goods, so his planned abundance cannot secure a remaining possession.
The parable's conclusion contrasts laying up treasure for oneself with being rich toward God, a moral qualification of what counts as valuable wealth.
Generosity stores a good foundation for the future and takes hold of true life, connecting cleanly directed wealth, self-giving, and an enduring good.
The mishnah names deeds whose fruits are enjoyed now while their principal remains for the world to come, a precise Jewish account of good that remains.
Sirach calls kindness a blessed garden and says almsgiving endures forever, joining the commentary's remaining goodness to generosity rather than accumulation.
Moses chooses mistreatment with God's people over temporary enjoyment of sin, a direct scriptural action of preferring a costly better good.
Moses judges reproach greater wealth than Egypt's treasures because he looks to the reward; Pharaoh's sphere becomes the setting for a valuation unlike the fleeting ruler's power.
The Judean officials refuse the king's gods and image even if God does not rescue them; like the commentary's magicians before Pharaoh, they choose fidelity under royal threat.
The Hebrew midwives fear God and disobey Pharaoh's order to kill boys, another Mosaic-world instance in which divine fear defeats a ruler's temporary command.
The apostles state that they must obey God rather than humans, a concise Christian formulation of the threatened preference enacted in the commentary's Pharaoh scene.
Grass withers and flower fades under the LORD's breath; its pasture-to-fading image is a close companion to 87:5 and the commentary's worldly flower.
Against fading grass and flower, God's word stands forever, supplying the lasting side needed by the commentary's vegetation-and-abiding contrast.

Peter reapplies Isaiah's grass image to all flesh and human glory: grass withers and its flower falls. This makes transient human status explicit beside the commentary's grass and lowly-human imagery.
Peter's continuation says the Lord's word remains forever and identifies it with the preached good news, interpreting the fading-grass contrast as a durable divine message.
The rich person's humiliation is likened to a flower of grass that passes away, directly tying social wealth to the commentary's flowerlike worldly life.
Sun and heat wither grass, drop its flower, and destroy its beauty; James applies that process to the rich person's pursuits, closely matching the meadow's discarded end.
Human days are grass and a person's flourishing is a field flower, a direct parallel for the commentary's flower image of worldly life.
After the wind passes, the flower is gone and its place knows it no more; this adds a specific fading-and-forgetting counterpart to the commentary's forgotten residue.
The LORD's steadfast love is from everlasting to everlasting, giving the psalm's answer to its prior grass-and-flower transience.
The wicked are chaff that the wind drives away, a pointed ethical use of plant refuse beside the commentary's discarded ghutha' and lower-human comparison.

column5: poor raised from dust and ash heap
column6: Rather than leaving the lowly among refuse, the psalm says God raises the poor from dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap; it reverses the commentary's social application of debris.
God chooses what the world calls low and despised to nullify what is; this directly counters an inference that social lowliness marks what should be discarded.
God chooses the poor in the world as rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom, reversing worldly rank while preserving the commentary's horizon of enduring inheritance.
The high and exalted God also dwells with the crushed and lowly to revive them, challenging any simple equation of low status with refuse.
God leaves a humble, lowly people who seek refuge in his name, joining low status to the positive remnant rather than to discard.
Israel's remnant does no wrong and speaks no lies; it gives the commentary's “remaining ones” a concrete moral profile.
God leaves seven thousand who have not bowed to Baal, a surviving moral remnant that resists corruption as the commentary's baqiyya image does.
The remnant no longer relies on its oppressor but relies faithfully on the LORD, specifying the faithful orientation of a remaining group.
After prosperity lifts the heart, Israel may forget the LORD; this supplies a concrete biblical form of the commentary's worldly preference joined to forgetting.
Agur fears that being full will lead him to deny God, giving the commentary's question of worldly wealth a particular spiritual danger.

column5: life and good / death and evil
column6: Moses sets life and good against death and evil, an explicit scriptural scale for the commentary's claim that choice seeks what is better.
The command to choose life turns evaluation into an accountable act, as the commentary turns preferring the lower worldly side into blameworthy choice.
Esau eats, drinks, and despises his birthright; the narrative makes a one-meal preference over an inheritance a concrete warning about choosing the immediate.
Hebrews interprets Esau's sale of the birthright for one meal as profane conduct, making the Genesis choice an ethical reading relevant to the commentary's sorting of choices.
Hebrews adds that Esau later seeks the blessing with tears but cannot reverse the result, stressing the lasting cost of his short-term exchange.
Solomon does not ask for long life, riches, or enemies' lives, but discernment for justice; his choice gives a narrative instance of seeking a higher good.

column5: money for what does not satisfy
column6: Isaiah asks why money and labor are spent on what does not satisfy, then calls listeners to eat what is good; it closely fits the commentary's scrutiny of valuable provision.
The proverb judges a little with righteousness better than large income with injustice, qualifying the commentary's abundance criterion by making moral source decisive.
The small portion of the righteous is better than the abundance of many wicked, another direct reversal of an amount-based account of good wealth.

column5: little with fear / treasure with turmoil
column6: A little with fear of the LORD is better than great treasure with turmoil, comparing material plenty with the quality of the life that holds it.
A good name is chosen over great riches and favor over silver and gold, directly depicting selection by worth rather than mere material quantity.
The worry of the age and deceitfulness of wealth choke the word and make it fruitless, a specific New Testament account of worldly preference producing spiritual waste.
The rich are told not to set hope on uncertain wealth but on God, turning the commentary's hierarchy of goods into an instruction about trust.

column5: feast for those unable to repay
column6: Jesus tells a host to invite poor, crippled, lame, and blind people rather than reciprocal guests, a practical enactment of preferring another's need over self-advantage.
Because such guests cannot repay, God repays the host at the resurrection of the righteous; generosity is explicitly joined to the lasting future.
Humility requires regarding others as surpassing oneself, directly corresponding to the commentary's explanation of preferring another over oneself.
Each person is told to attend to others' interests as well as personal interests, supplying a concrete ethical form for right-directed preference.
The instruction not to seek one's own interest but that of the other gives a compact analogue to the commentary's positive sense of ithar.

column5: repentance and deeds in this world
column6: The first half of the same maxim says an hour of repentance and good deeds here is better than all the coming world; it complicates the commentary by valuing this life as the place of moral action.
Israel is chosen not for numerical abundance but despite being the fewest people, offering a counterpoint to reading selectness through quantity or social rank.
God rejects human sight of outward appearance and looks at the heart; it reframes the commentary's language of low value and selection around hidden moral reality.
Paul's remembered saying of Jesus calls giving more blessed than receiving, a concise valuation of self-giving alongside the commentary's positive preference of others.

column5: foreign city and one's future city
column6: Hermas treats believers as residents of a foreign city who should not build their hopes there because their proper city lies elsewhere; it develops the present-world versus lasting-destination image.
The homily calls the flesh's stay in this world brief and transient and sets it beside Christ's promised coming kingdom and eternal life, closely echoing the commentary's contrast.

column5: things to use and things to enjoy
column6: Augustine distinguishes temporary things used on the way from God, who is to be enjoyed as beatitude; this interpretive hierarchy clarifies what a rightly ordered preference can mean.

Genesis explains Manasseh's name with Hebrew nashani, “has made me forget,” about Joseph's hardship. It is a likely Semitic cognate of the commentary's nasiya label, though the Genesis scene contains no debris image.
